knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

## Question 1 Approach

We use a scatter plot to present the relationship between content age on Netflix and views. This plot is suitable because it can display two numerical variables and allows us to identify patterns in the data. We also add a smooth trend line to show the relationship and use facets to compare movies and shows separately.

For the second plot, we use a point-range plot to compare views across different content age groups. This plot is suitable because it presents each group’s viewing performance and variability. It is easier to compare differences between age groups. We use the median to represent typical views and the interquartile range to show the spread of the observations. We also use facets to separate movies and shows.

## Question 1 Analysis

```{r Question1 Analysis, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# install.packages("ggplot2")
# install.packages("tidyverse")
# install.packages("scales")
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

# Load the datasets.
movies <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-07-29/movies.csv')
shows <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-07-29/shows.csv')

# Combine the movies and shows datasets and remove missing release_date values.
q1_netflix <- bind_rows(
  movies %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Movie") %>% 
    filter(!is.na(release_date)),
  shows %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Show") %>% 
    filter(!is.na(release_date))
)

# Convert release_date to Date format and use the end date of each reporting period to calculate the content's age on Netflix. 
# Calculate the age by subtracting release_date from report_end_date, then convert it to years for easier interpretation on the x-axis.
q1_netflix <- q1_netflix %>%
  mutate(
    release_date = as.Date(release_date),
    
    # Create a column for the end date of each reporting period. Keep the first four characters (the year) and replace the remaining part with the corresponding end date.
    report_end_date = case_when(
      str_detect(report, "Jan-Jun") ~
        as.Date(paste0(str_sub(report, 1, 4), "-06-30")), 
      str_detect(report, "Jul-Dec") ~
        as.Date(paste0(str_sub(report, 1, 4), "-12-31"))
      ),
    content_netflix_age_days =
      as.numeric(report_end_date - release_date),
    content_netflix_age =
      content_netflix_age_days / 365
  )
```

```{r Question1 Figure1, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(
  q1_netflix,
  aes(x = content_netflix_age,
      y = views
     )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.15,
    size = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Add a smooth trend line to show the relationship between content age and views.
  # se = FALSE removes the confidence interval shading.
  geom_smooth( 
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  
  # Create separate panels for movies and shows.
  facet_grid(
    . ~ content_type
  ) +
  
  # Use a base-10 logarithmic scale for the y-axis and display values with commas.
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = label_comma()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Netflix Content Age and Views",
    x = "Years Since Netflix Release",
    y = "Views (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r Question1 Figure2, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Group views by content age to compare viewing performance across age groups.
age_summary_2 <- q1_netflix %>%
  
  # Keep records with valid content age and positive views.
  filter(
    content_netflix_age >= 0,
    views > 0
  ) %>%
  
  # Divide content into age groups based on years since Netflix release.
  mutate(
    age_group = cut(
      content_netflix_age,
      
      # Define the boundaries for each age group.'Inf' represents positive infinity, allowing the last group to include all values greater than or equal to 10.
      breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 5, 10, Inf),
      
      # Exclude the right boundary of each interval.
      right = FALSE,
      labels = c(
        "<1 year",
        "1-<3 years",
        "3-<5 years",
        "5-<10 years",
        "10+ years"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Group records by content type and age group.
  group_by(content_type, age_group) %>%
  
  # Calculate the number of records, median views, and the 25th and 75th percentiles.
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_views = median(views),
    q25 = quantile(views, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(views, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot the median views as points and use vertical lines to show the interquartile range.
ggplot(
  age_summary_2,
  aes(
    x = age_group,
    y = median_views
  )
) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      ymin = q25, # Set the lower end of the range to the 25th percentile.
      ymax = q75  # Set the upper end of the range to the 75th percentile.
    )
  ) +
  
  # Create separate panels for movies and shows.
  facet_grid(. ~ content_type) +
  
  # Customize the x-axis labels and add line breaks to improve readability.
  scale_x_discrete(
      labels = c(
        "<1 year",
        "1-<3\nyears",
        "3-<5\nyears",
        "5-<10\nyears",
        "10+ years"
      )
  ) + 
  
  # Use a base-10 logarithmic scale for the y-axis and display values with commas.
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = label_comma()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Views by Time Since Netflix Release",
    x = "Years Since Netflix Release",
    y = "Views (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
## Question 2 Approach

For the first plot, we have created a ridge plot for a cursory look at the frequency of view counts across shows and movies on Netflix that are either globally available or region-locked. This plot enables us to find immediate patterns in the distribution of views that shows and movies get based on if the content is available globally or not.

For the second plot, we take a closer look at the viewcounts via violin box plot. This way we can directly compare viewcounts between globally available and region-locked shows and movies via measures of central tendency such as median while still retaining an idea of the distributions that each category displays.

## Question 2 Analysis
```{r Question2 Analysis, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#install.packages("tidytuesdayR")
#install.packages("ggplot2")
#install.packages("scales")
#install.packages("tidyverse")
#install.packages("ggridges")
library(ggridges)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidytuesdayR)

# Load datasets
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load('2025-07-29')
movies <- tuesdata$movies
shows <- tuesdata$shows

# Remove entries with missing viewcount and global availability data
movies_clean <- movies %>%
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(views))

shows_clean <- shows %>%
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(views))

# Combine movie and show datasets
q2_netflix <- bind_rows(
  movies_clean %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Movie"),
  shows_clean %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Show"))
```

```{r Question2 Figure1, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(q2_netflix,
       aes(x = views,
           y = available_globally,
           fill = available_globally)) +
  # Display view axis values using log-10 scale and change from scientific notation to commas
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  # Separate movies and shows into different graphs
  facet_grid( . ~ content_type) +
  labs(
    title = "Frequency of Viewcounts for Globally Available and Region-locked Movies and Shows on Netflix",
    x = "Views (log scale)",
    y = "Global Availability"
  )
```

```{r Question2 Figure2, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(q2_netflix,
       aes(x = available_globally,
           y = views)) +
  # Display view axis values using log-10 scale and change from scientific notation to commas
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  geom_violin(fill = "green3") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.05) +
  # Separate movies and shows into different graphs
  facet_grid( . ~ content_type) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Viewcounts for Globally Available and Region-locked Movies and Shows on Netflix",
    x = "Global Availability",
    y = "Views (log scale)"
  )
```
